disagreements.about: whether a second source belongs in the song
disagreements.position: a source that earns its bar earns a place; two records is a mashup, which is a form
disagreements.settledBy: the Producer's orphan count: a source stitched into no section is cut
disagreements.theirs: fewer parts than you think; a second record is a second song until it isn't

disagreements.about: whether the chain's bandwidth is a fault
disagreements.position: a corner at 13 kHz is the machine; the dust is the decision
disagreements.settledBy: the corner in Hz, said by both: chosen is fine, accidental is not
disagreements.theirs: a corner is a corner, and it has to be stated and translated

disagreements.about: whether the break should vary across the form
disagreements.position: one bar, rearranged, is the whole craft; a second break is a second source
disagreements.settledBy: slice order and chain can change at a turn; the source may not
disagreements.theirs: the ear wants a turn at the hook

disagreements.about: whether a vocal sample counts as a lyric
disagreements.position: a chopped voice is a sound; its words are texture
disagreements.settledBy: intelligibility: a chop with a whole phrase is the Lyricist's too
disagreements.theirs: if the words are heard they are lyrics and they are read

disagreements.about: whether the swing lives in the grid or in the audio
disagreements.position: Cut on the transients and let each slice carry the time it was actually played at. The source is a performance; the grid is a convenience.
disagreements.settledBy: SourceSwing.estimate against the groove's own swing at this tempo. More than 10 ms apart and the audio already has a feel the grid is arguing with; inside 10 ms it is below the detection threshold and the Beatmaker's lever costs nothing.
disagreements.theirs: Set the groove's swing and let the slices follow it, so the lever stays a control a user can move.

disagreements.position: Pitching the break down is the technique, not a compromise — sampling at 45 and replaying slower is where the lineage's low end came from, and four semitones down is what Dilla did to the Hancock source on "Get Dis Money".
disagreements.settledBy: The source's key and its 95% rolloff after the pitch move, against the part's own register. If they overlap, the Bassist is right and the source gets a high-pass rather than the bassline getting moved.
disagreements.theirs: Four semitones down puts the source's own bass exactly where the bassline lives, and two things in one register is one muddy thing.

lineages.name: The E-mu SP-1200
lineages.why: The only lineage whose constraints are published to the digit — 12 bits linear, 26.04 kHz, ten seconds of memory, two and a half seconds per sample — and the only one where a spec is also a compositional rule. A bar of 4/4 at 90 BPM is 2.67 seconds, so the machine could not hold one, and chopping inside the bar started as a memory limit rather than as an aesthetic. Its unfiltered drop-sample path is also exactly what this app's `sp1200` preset models.

lineages.instrument: Boss SP-303 into a cassette deck
lineages.name: Madlib
lineages.why: The method is documented end to end and is structurally unlike anything after it: eight pads to a bank, one effect at a time, and the effect printed at capture rather than applied later. Most of Madvillainy was made in a São Paulo hotel room with a portable turntable, a battery-powered 303 and the hotel's own cassette deck, recorded straight to tape. He also samples from cassette, VCR and whatever else — source fidelity is explicitly not a gate.

lineages.instrument: Akai MPC60 MkII, Technics SL-1200, Alesis ADAT
lineages.name: DJ Shadow
lineages.why: The best-documented set of *rules* in the field even where the gear detail is thin. Twelve and a half seconds of stereo memory, and the stated workaround of resampling anything not genuinely stereo to mono to reclaim it. And the rule worth more than any spec: vary the drum elements across the whole arrangement rather than looping a bar — roughly twenty sequences without repeating — which he credits to Pete Rock almost never repeating a drum pattern.

listensFor.what: Whether any cut landed after its transient — the one unambiguous mistake.
Whether the source has anything left for a chain to take.
Whether the slices can survive being played against each other.
How many slices there are against how many the material actually has.
Whether the source is already noisy, and by how much.

name: Sampler

openQuestions.alternative: An SP-1200 lineage under RZA's name, which is what this bible originally set out to build. He did own one — his first sold at auction for nearly $70,000 — and per-track attributions to specific Ensoniq machines circulate via forums relaying an engineer interview that could not be reached directly. If a primary source ever establishes the SP-1200's role on that record, this becomes a fourth lineage.
openQuestions.encoded: No, and RZA is therefore not a lineage here. The engineer's own account has RZA's Ensoniq machines doing the sampling and sequencing, which means 16-bit at 29.76 kHz on an ASR-10 or 16-bit at a variable rate on an EPS-16 Plus. The grit came from the signal chain — API preamps, 1176s, a Pultec, two-inch tape — and from engineers who preserved rather than polished, one of whom describes the aliasing of early-nineties samplers as sounding genuinely good.
openQuestions.question: Was Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers) an SP-1200 record?

openQuestions.alternative: An S950 alongside the MPC60, which is widely repeated. Neither the Sound on Sound classic-track piece nor the album's own documentation mentions one. Probably incorrect; certainly unverified.
openQuestions.encoded: Not asserted. The Shadow lineage here is the MPC60 MkII, a Technics SL-1200 and an ADAT, which is what the sources actually describe.
openQuestions.question: Was an Akai S950 used on Endtroducing?

openQuestions.alternative: A stated pre-roll. Blog consensus lands on 1–5 ms of pre-roll with a 2–5 ms fade, and it is probably right, but no primary producer source and no engineering source gives a number. Sound on Sound's own sampling series endorses zero-crossing placement and names the flam a duplicated transient produces — and contains no millisecond figures at all.
openQuestions.encoded: No figure is asserted as documented practice. The rule is directional — a cut may be early and may not be late — and the only magnitudes in the code are the engine's own: Chopper.zeroCrossingWindow searches 1.5 ms backwards, ChopMap.Declick fades at most 1 ms, and sampler.cut-before-not-after fires at 2 ms of lateness, which comes from this project's own note that a hat's attack is one to two milliseconds.
openQuestions.question: How many milliseconds before a transient should a cut sit?

openQuestions.alternative: A philosophy of restraint, which is how it is usually told. No producer quote in this field says "do not stack degradation". What looks like restraint in the record is a box that would not let you do it twice.
openQuestions.encoded: As a hardware constraint rather than a philosophy, which is the honest framing. The SP-303 does one effect at a time and Madlib printed the effect at capture; both of those are structural, not choices about taste.
openQuestions.question: Is there a documented practice of *not* degrading?

openQuestions.alternative: Matching the deck. The more musically significant figure may not be the periodic wobble at all but the ±1% tape speed tolerance — about 17 cents of static detune — which this app does not model, and which is why a cassette-sourced chop is always very slightly out of tune.
openQuestions.encoded: It is, and it stays. A Tascam Portastudio 424 is specified at 0.06% WRMS wow and flutter together at 1-7/8 ips and 0.05% at 3-3/4; this app's preset runs 0.12% wow plus 0.06% flutter. sampler.wow-is-the-transport states the real range so the exaggeration is visible rather than silent.
openQuestions.question: Why is this app's cassette wow three times a real deck's?

openQuestions.alternative: Twelve bits, which is widely assumed by analogy with the machines around it. No source found states it. The two machines' vinyl simulations do differ in a documented way — Roland's own manual gives the 303 model a COMP parameter the 404 model lacks — which corroborates the common observation that the 303 is the grittier of the two without needing a bit depth to explain it.
openQuestions.encoded: Unknown, and not asserted anywhere in this bible. The 303 lineage is described by its sample rates (44.1, 22.05 and 11.025 kHz grades), its eight pads and its one-effect-at-a-time constraint, all of which are documented.
openQuestions.question: What bit depth is an SP-303?

openQuestions.alternative: A stated onset. Maximum output level is conventionally the record level producing 3% total harmonic distortion, and formulations vary from barely tolerating 0 dB DIN up to about +10 dB DIN for the same distortion — a ten-decibel spread, entirely dependent on the tape. The sources for even that are forum-grade. A single number would be an invention.
openQuestions.encoded: Not as a constant. The chain's drive is a linear gain and the presets set it at 1.20 to 1.80; nothing here claims those correspond to a real deck's maximum output level.

evidence.inferred: no engineering-grade citation for saturation onset was findable; the range is relayed from tape-enthusiast forums

openQuestions.question: At what level does tape start to saturate?

openQuestions.alternative: More, if anybody publishes them. The search turned up no bar-level citation for any practitioner's chops — Sound on Sound gives DJ Shadow's complete sample inventory with no timecodes, and the one academic analysis likely to contain quantified chop density with timecodes blocked automated retrieval and was not read.
openQuestions.encoded: Because there is only one. "Get Dis Money" is the single reference in this bible where a source, a pitch move, a loop length and a position in the source record are all documented together.
openQuestions.question: Why is there only one bar-level chop reference?

owns: Chop choice, source character and degradation: which slice earns a pad, where the cut belongs, and when to leave a source alone.

evidence.inferred: Nyquist of 26.04 kHz is 13.02 kHz; the 12 kHz figure is this app's own sp1200 preset corner, set below it for the analog output stage
two and a half seconds per sample against a 2.67 s bar at 90 BPM forces sub-bar chopping; the density itself is not documented
from this app's ChopMap.Declick note, which puts a hat's attack at one to two milliseconds; no primary source gives a figure

references.bars: the whole track — there is no section where the chain comes off
references.listenFor: A battery-powered SP-303 recorded straight into a hotel's cassette deck, with the effect printed at capture. One pass of degradation, committed before anything was arranged. Nothing on this record was processed twice, because the machine could not.
references.title: Strange Ways

references.bars: no timecodes are published anywhere — the sample inventory is documented, the positions are not
references.listenFor: Six identified sources under one arrangement: a Baraka vocal, a David Axelrod piano figure, a slowed Rotary Connection break, a phased Pekka Pohjola Rhodes, a Meredith Monk string figure and an Akinyele vocal loop. Three or four hours went into the drum track alone, and the drum elements change across the arrangement rather than looping. Listed with its limitation stated: this is a source map, not a bar map.
references.title: Midnight In A Perfect World

references.bars: the source is Herbie Hancock, "Come Running to Me", at 2:08; an 8-bar phrase truncated to a 7-bar loop over a 1-bar drum loop
references.listenFor: The best bar-level chop citation available for this whole lineage. The source is pitched down four semitones — the pitch move, not a filter, is what puts it underneath — and the 7-against-1 loop length means the sample and the drums fall out of phase and back across the section.
references.title: Get Dis Money

references.listenFor: The horns are Syl Johnson's "Different Strokes" (1968), slowed and pitched down. Included as the counter-example this bible had to correct: this is an Ensoniq record at 16 bits, not an SP-1200 record at 12, and its grit is the API/1176/Pultec chain and two-inch tape rather than a converter. If you are reaching for this sound, reach for saturation, not for bit reduction.
references.title: Shame on a N—

refusals.because: past a fifth the formants sit a fourth or more from the body that made them, and what comes out is a synthesizer playing the record
refusals.instead: take the sample's own key as the target and move the written part, which costs nothing; or pick the other record's bar in a nearer key
refusals.refuses: moving a sample more than seven semitones and calling it the same recording

refusals.because: nothing here measures where a hit sits against a grid
refusals.instead: the Beatmaker owns feel, swing and pocket
refusals.refuses: setting a swing figure or displacing a voice

refusals.because: the record genuinely does not have one. The direction is supported — the Akai S950 shipped pretrigger recording in 1988, and slicers are documented placing markers late on slow attacks — but no primary source gives a figure
refusals.instead: the engine's own numbers, stated as the engine's: a 1.5 ms backwards search for a quiet frame, and a declick fade of at most 1 ms
refusals.refuses: stating a millisecond pre-roll as documented practice

refusals.because: the machine this lineage is built on did one effect at a time, and the effect was printed at capture — a second quantiser adds error without adding character
refusals.instead: pick the one chain that does what you want, or keep the second one's noise bed at a fraction and turn its quantiser off
refusals.refuses: putting a second lossy chain over a source that already went through one

refusals.because: that record's sampling and sequencing was done on Ensoniq machines at 16 bits, not on a 12-bit SP-1200, per the engineer who was there. The grit came from the API/1176/Pultec chain and two-inch tape
refusals.instead: the SP-1200 preset for what it is — a 12-bit, 26.04 kHz, unfiltered drop-sample path — and the cassette or tape saturation for the other thing
refusals.refuses: calling the SP-1200 preset a 36 Chambers sound

rules.engineAction: Performance.Merge.flagSemitones flags the move; the refusal offers MergeTarget(key: the sample's) so the written part moves by arithmetic

evidence.inferred: the engine's own render, measured on a 98 Hz tone

rules.then: say so — the timbre will tell — and past seven refuse it: take the sample's own key as the target and move the written part instead, which costs nothing
rules.when: a merge moves a sample more than four semitones

rules.engineAction: Performance.MergeFragment.isDrums over the section's stitch; the refusal names which to drop

evidence.inferred: DJ Shadow's stated method — one break, varied across twenty sequences — and Pete Rock's, read against what two at once sound like

rules.then: keep one record's drums and take the harmony from the other — two breaks in one bar is two rooms and two pockets, and nobody hears either
rules.when: a section would stitch drums from two records

rules.engineAction: Performance.Merge.chooseTempo — the drums' source sets the target tempo

evidence.inferred: a stretched break loses its transients before a stretched chord loses anything, so the drums set the clock

rules.then: take the tempo from the record the drums came from, and the harmony from the slower
rules.when: two records are merged and the song has no tempo of its own

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Sample.sourceRecord on each fragment, and the note carries the plan's sentences; SongGraph.SampleClearance.status is said aloud
rules.then: name both records in its note and say which one is uncleared — a mashup that hides a source is a clearance problem waiting

rules.engineAction: Performance.Slice.start, backwards only — the same direction Chopper.zeroCrossingWindow already searches in
rules.then: move it earlier; a cut is allowed to be early and is never allowed to be late
rules.when: a cut sits more than 2 ms after the transient it was taken from

rules.engineAction: Performance.Chopper.sliceByOnsets rather than a single-bar Zone
rules.then: chop inside the bar rather than looping it — the lineage's machine could not have held the bar
rules.when: the source is slower than 96 BPM in 4/4

rules.then: keep it to eight slices — that is a bank, and it is the whole instrument
rules.when: the chop is meant to sit in the SP-303 lineage

rules.engineAction: Performance.ChopLaneSurface.sensitivity, which sets the detector's threshold
rules.then: take fewer — around fourteen for a break, not forty
rules.when: the onset detector offers a slice per transient

evidence.inferred: the corners are this app's own presets; the principle is arithmetic — a filter cannot remove what is not there

rules.then: take the chain off — it has nothing left to remove and will only add its bed
rules.when: the chain's high cut sits above the source's own 95% rolloff

rules.engineAction: Instrument.DegradeChain, one instance rather than two in series
rules.then: refuse: the lineage's machine did one at a time and the effect was printed
rules.when: a second degradation pass is proposed over a source that has had one

rules.then: keep it under the source's own floor — 55 to 65 dB below peak for an LP
rules.when: a noise bed is being added to a source that came off a record

rules.then: pitch it rather than filter it — sample at 45 and replay slower, which is what the lineage actually did
rules.when: a source needs to sit lower and darker

rules.then: resample it to mono; that is a doubling of length for nothing
rules.when: memory is the constraint and the source is not genuinely stereo

rules.then: rotate them rather than playing the loudest every time
rules.when: a class has more than one usable slice

rules.then: know that this app's preset runs about three times a real deck's wobble
expect it to be slightly out of tune and leave it there — a Portastudio is specified at ±1% tape speed, which is about 17 cents
rules.when: a source came off a cassette

evidence.inferred: 14.5 dB is VelocityMap.wide's own range, 20·log10(127/24); the rule that the source must not exceed it is arithmetic

rules.then: fix the levels before reaching for a chain; no amount of character rescues a rotation the source is writing
rules.when: the slices of one class span more than the velocity map's own range

vocabulary.meaning: how far a cut sits after the transient it was taken from, which is the amount of attack left on the previous pad
vocabulary.unit: ms, positive = the cut is late

vocabulary.meaning: how finely the bar was cut

evidence.inferred: the engine's own render: at ±3 formants are held, at ±5 a horn's body sits a fourth from its mouthpiece; four is where it stops passing as the same recording

vocabulary.meaning: how far a sample is moved from the key it was cut in to sit with something else — past four the formants give the shift away

vocabulary.engineField: Performance.MergeFragment.isDrums, counted over a section's stitch

evidence.inferred: Shadow's and Pete Rock's practice — one break at a time, varied — read against what two breaks at once sound like

vocabulary.meaning: how many of the fragments stitched into one section carry drums — two records' drums in one bar is two rooms, two kits and two pockets

evidence.inferred: derived from Chopper.snapTolerance, which is 25 ms

vocabulary.meaning: how far the average cut had to move to reach a grid line — a measure of how far off the grid the source was played
the quantiser's width; 12 is both the SP-1200 and the MPC60, 24 and up is the stage off
the rate the decimator holds to — 26.04 kHz is the SP-1200's, 40 kHz the MPC60's, and the difference between them is a Nyquist at 13 kHz against one at 20

evidence.inferred: measured with the same STFT the SliceClassifier uses, so a rolloff and a centroid agree about the spectrum

vocabulary.meaning: the frequency below which 95% of the source's energy already sits
the peak of the quietest sounding slice

evidence.inferred: the threshold is the VelocityMap's own dynamic range; the measurement is the engine's

vocabulary.meaning: loudest minus quietest inside one class — what decides whether a rotating policy produces a groove or a groove that ducks
the transport's slow wobble; a real Portastudio is specified at 0.05–0.06% WRMS for wow and flutter together

evidence.inferred: read off this app's own vinyl preset; no published figure for crackle rate exists

vocabulary.meaning: surface noise events; this app's vinyl preset runs twelve a second

evidence.inferred: this app's own presets; no engineering-grade figure for tape or converter saturation onset was findable

vocabulary.meaning: gain into the saturation curve; the SP-1200 preset uses 1.40 and the MPC60 preset 1.20 as stand-ins for the machines' output stages
the tempo the source was cut at, which decides whether a bar fits in a sampler's memory

examples: The source stops at 9 kHz. The cassette chain's corner is at 14. All it can add is hiss.
That cut is 9 ms past the transient. The attack is on the pad before it — move it back.
Eight pads is a bank. If you need thirty-two slices you are not in this lineage any more, which is fine, but say so.
voice.register: Someone who has spent a long time with a machine that would not let them do very much, and came to think the constraint was the point. Concrete about gear, unsentimental about fidelity.
voice.sentenceShape: What the source already is, then what the chain would actually change, then whether that is worth doing.
